content: FAN1, also known as FANCD2/FANCI-associated nuclease 1 (KIAA1018), is an enzyme encoded by the FAN1 gene in humans. It functions as a structure-dependent endonuclease and belongs to the myotubularin-related class 1 cysteine-based protein tyrosine phosphatases. FAN1 is believed to play a critical role in the Fanconi Anemia (FA) DNA repair pathway. Structure of FAN1 FAN1 is a protein composed of 1017 amino acids. Several crystal structures of its residues, specifically from 373 to 1017, have been characterized. This region of FAN1 contains three distinct domains: 1. SAP domain: This is the primary DNA-binding domain. It consists of three major components—α9, α5β1, and α7. The α9 helix stabilizes the protein during dimerization and mediates interactions between α5β1 and α7 as they adjust their positions. These configurations allow FAN1 to transition through substrate scanning, substrate latching, and substrate unwinding states. 2. TPR domain: This domain facilitates interdomain interactions and forms the dimerization interface. 3. VRR_NUC domain: This is the catalytic site, also known as the virus-type replication-repair nuclease module. FAN1 binds to DNA in a head-to-tail dimeric configuration. The SAP domains of both FAN1 molecules in the dimer interact with the DNA duplex, which promotes DNA-induced dimerization and guides single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) into the SAP domain of the downstream enzyme. The SAP domain of the upstream enzyme assists in directing DNA to the downstream enzyme. The SAP domain's surface near the catalytic site is highly conserved among FAN1 homologs and is positively charged, enabling favorable hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions with DNA. Specific residues, such as Y374 and Y436, form hydrogen bonds with the DNA phosphate backbone. FAN1 can bind DNA in either orientation. However, if the 5' flap of the DNA is positioned away from the VRR_NUC catalytic site, substrate latching and unwinding cannot occur. The unresolved N-terminal portion of FAN1 contains a Zinc finger domain, known as the UBZ region, which is highly conserved across eukaryotes. This domain is essential for recruiting FAN1 to the ubiquitinated FANCD2/FANCI complex. The VRR_NUC domain, located at the C-terminus, provides the endonuclease activity. FAN1 is the first known example of a virus-type replication-repair nuclease module in eukaryotes, a domain typically found in bacterial and viral Holliday Junction Resolvases (HJRs). However, FAN1 does not exhibit activity on Holliday Junction substrates, likely due to an inhibitory subdomain of SAP connected to the VRR_NUC region. Function of FAN1 Interstrand DNA crosslinks (ICLs) are highly toxic lesions that block the progression of transcription and replication machinery. To resolve these blocks, a process called unhooking is required, which involves incising one strand of the DNA duplex on either side of the ICL. FAN1 plays a critical role in this repair process, which is initiated when a replication fork stalls at an ICL. The Fanconi Anemia (FA) pathway involves 15 known proteins that work together to remove ICLs. The FA pathway begins with the FA AP24-MHF1/2 complex recognizing the ICL at the stalled replication fork. This complex recruits the FA core complex, which consists of eight proteins. The core complex monoubiquitinates FANCD2 and FANCI, enabling them to form a heterodimer. This heterodimer then recruits FAN1 and other nucleases, such as SLX4. Ubiquitinated FANCD2 interacts directly with FAN1, which is recruited to the site of damage. FAN1 restrains DNA replication fork progression and prevents chromosomal abnormalities when replication forks stall. FAN1 is primarily localized in the nucleus but forms distinct foci at sites of DNA damage when ICLs are present. It possesses both endonuclease and exonuclease activities, enabling it to remove ICLs. At a replication fork arrested by an ICL, FAN1 catalyzes incisions in the double-stranded DNA, unhooking the crosslink and separating the DNA strands. This process generates one strand with a crosslinked nucleotide and another strand with a gap. FAN1 preferentially acts as a 5' flap endonuclease, cleaving approximately five nucleotides from a junction. It can also incise at splayed arms, three-way junctions, and 3' flaps, though with decreasing preference. At high concentrations, FAN1 exhibits 3' to 5' exonuclease activity. FAN1 does not bind to single-stranded DNA. The presence of the FANCD2/FANCI complex is not affected by FAN1 knockdown, as FAN1 functions downstream of FANCD2/FANCI recruitment. FAN1 has also been shown to increase the frequency of homologous recombination (HR), suggesting that the gapped intermediate formed after ICL unhooking may be repaired through HR when homologous chromosomes are available. FAN1 does not appear to participate in other types of DNA repair, as it does not localize to DNA damage sites following irradiation. Clinical Significance of FAN1 Mutations in any of the 15 known FA genes are associated with Fanconi Anemia, a rare autosomal recessive disorder. This condition is characterized by congenital abnormalities, bone marrow failure, anemia, and a predisposition to cancer during childhood. However, some patients with Fanconi Anemia do not have mutations in the known FA genes, a condition referred to as unassigned Fanconi Anemia. Mutations in FAN1 have been linked to chronic kidney diseases and neurological disorders such as schizophrenia. However, recent studies have questioned whether FAN1 should be classified as an FA gene. In 2015, researchers studied four individuals with chromosomal microdeletions in the 15q13.3 region, which includes FAN1. Blood sample analysis revealed only mild sensitivity to ICL-inducing agents and chromosomal fragility consistent with Fanconi Anemia. FAN1 deficiency increases sensitivity to crosslinking agents such as cisplatin and mitomycin C in vitro. FAN1 is also capable of repairing double-strand breaks induced by mitomycin C. Germline mutations in the FAN1 gene have been implicated in hereditary colorectal cancer, likely due to defective DNA repair mechanisms.
